beats.caption: Book-to-bill compares new orders to what was shipped and billed
beats.text: Bookings are new orders signed in a period; billings are products shipped and invoiced in the same period. Book-to-bill is bookings divided by billings. A chip-tool maker that booked $12B and billed $10B in a quarter has a ratio of 1.2.

beats.caption: Above 1.0, orders outrun shipments and the backlog grows
beats.text: When customers order faster than the factory can build and ship, unfilled orders pile up as backlog. A ratio above 1 means future revenue is already being locked in, and lead times usually stretch.

beats.caption: Below 1.0, shipments outrun orders and the backlog drains
beats.text: When orders slow, the plant keeps shipping out of its backlog, so revenue can look fine for a while even as new business dries up. A ratio stuck below 1 warns that revenue will fall once the backlog runs down.

beats.caption: It turns before revenue, which is why investors watch it
beats.text: Because orders come months before shipments, the ratio tends to turn ahead of reported sales. Equipment and chip makers have long published it as a read on demand; a single quarter can be lumpy when one big customer places a large order.

beats.caption: Chip-equipment makers are where the number matters most
beats.text: Fabs order lithography, etch and test tools a year or more ahead, so tool makers' orders and backlog lead the whole cycle. Some now report backlog instead of a strict ratio, but the idea is the same. Related: Applied Materials (AMAT), ASML (ASML), Lam Research (LRCX), Teradyne (TER).
